docs.title: Exploring the TheLook Ecommerce Dataset
docs.text: You are going to find and explore a public dataset in BigQuery. The dataset is a simulated ecommerce store - it has orders, products, customers, and more.

docs.title: Step 1: Find the dataset
docs.text:
In the BigQuery console, look at the Explorer panel on the left.

At the top of the Explorer panel, click the search icon and type:

thelook_ecommerce

In the results, you should see thelook_ecommerce under bigquery-public-data. Click the star icon next to it to pin it so it stays in your Explorer panel.

If you do not see a search icon, click + ADD DATA at the top of the Explorer panel, choose Pin a project, and type:

bigquery-public-data

Then expand bigquery-public-data in the Explorer panel and scroll down to find thelook_ecommerce.

docs.title: Step 2: Understand the structure
docs.text:
BigQuery organises everything in three levels:

Level What it is SSMS equivalent Project The top-level container - like a workspace or billing account Server Dataset A collection of related tables Database Table Rows and columns of data Table

In the Explorer panel you can see this hierarchy: ingwane-da4m3 > thelook_ecommerce > orders

That is: project > dataset > table. You will use this three-part path when writing queries.

docs.title: Step 3: Explore the tables
docs.text:
Expand the thelook_ecommerce dataset. You will see several tables:

Table What it contains orders One row per order - date, status, customer order_items One row per item within an order products The product catalogue - name, category, price users Customer records inventory_items Stock records events Website activity - clicks, page views distribution_centers Warehouse locations

docs.title: Step 4: Look at a table
docs.text:
Click on the orders table. You will see three tabs:

  • Schema - the columns and their data types
  • Details - row count, size, when it was last updated
  • Preview - a sample of the actual data

Work through each tab for orders, then do the same for order_items and products.

docs.title: Step 5: Questions to think about
docs.text:
As you explore, consider:

  • What does one row in orders represent?
  • What does one row in order_items represent?
  • How do you think orders and order_items are connected?
  • What columns look useful for analysis?

docs.title: Step 6: What else is in BigQuery public data?
docs.text:
If you pinned bigquery-public-data, scroll through the list in the Explorer panel - there are hundreds of datasets. You do not need to open them, but notice the range:

  • chicago_crime - crime reports from Chicago
  • covid19_open_data - global COVID-19 records
  • london_bicycles - London cycle hire trips
  • noaa_gsod - global weather station readings
  • wikipedia - Wikipedia page view data

This is one of the things that makes BigQuery different from a local database - large, real-world datasets are available to query immediately, with no setup.

docs.title: Step 7: Open the query editor
docs.text:
Click on the orders table, then click Query at the top of the table panel (or click the three dots next to the table and choose Query).

A SQL editor will open in the main panel. BigQuery will pre-fill the table name for you.

You do not need to run anything yet - just notice that the editor is there, it looks familiar, and the table reference is already in place. That is where you will work next.

docs.title: Running Queries in BigQuery
docs.text:
Your trainer will run each query and talk through the results. Follow along in your own editor - run the queries yourself as you go.

Check before you run

BigQuery charges based on how much data a query reads. Before you click Run, look at the top right of the editor - BigQuery will show you how much data the query will process (for example, "This query will process 1.2 GB when run").

Always use LIMIT when exploring data. A SELECT * with no limit on a large table can scan gigabytes unnecessarily.

For this course, the project has a budget set - but this is a habit worth building now.

docs.title: Part 1: Exploring the data
docs.text:
How many rows are in each table?

SELECT COUNT(*) FROM `bigquery-public-data.thelook_ecommerce.users`

SELECT COUNT(*) FROM `bigquery-public-data.thelook_ecommerce.orders`

Now preview some actual rows:

SELECT * FROM `bigquery-public-data.thelook_ecommerce.users` LIMIT 10

SELECT * FROM `bigquery-public-data.thelook_ecommerce.products` LIMIT 10

Notice the backtick syntax - project.dataset.table. This is how BigQuery identifies a table.

docs.title: Part 2: Filtering and sorting
docs.text:
Orders with a specific status:

SELECT *
FROM `bigquery-public-data.thelook_ecommerce.orders`
WHERE status = 'Shipped'
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 20

Products in a specific category:

SELECT name, brand, retail_price
FROM `bigquery-public-data.thelook_ecommerce.products`
WHERE category = 'Jeans'
ORDER BY retail_price DESC

WHERE and ORDER BY work exactly as they do in SSMS. The SQL is the same - only the table reference has changed.

docs.title: Part 3: Aggregations
docs.text:
Orders grouped by status:

SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS total_orders
FROM `bigquery-public-data.thelook_ecommerce.orders`
GROUP BY status
ORDER BY total_orders DESC

Average sale price by product category:

SELECT product_category, ROUND(AVG(sale_price), 2) AS avg_sale_price
FROM `bigquery-public-data.thelook_ecommerce.order_items`
GROUP BY product_category
ORDER BY avg_sale_price DESC

Top 10 brands by number of products:

SELECT brand, COUNT(*) AS num_products
FROM `bigquery-public-data.thelook_ecommerce.products`
GROUP BY brand
ORDER BY num_products DESC
LIMIT 10

docs.title: Part 4: Joining tables
docs.text:
Orders with the customer name added:

SELECT
  o.order_id,
  u.first_name,
  u.last_name,
  u.country,
  o.status,
  o.created_at
FROM `bigquery-public-data.thelook_ecommerce.orders` o
JOIN `bigquery-public-data.thelook_ecommerce.users` u
  ON o.user_id = u.id
LIMIT 20

The join works just as it does in SSMS - match a key in one table to a key in another. The only difference is the full project.dataset.table reference.

docs.title: What to notice
docs.text:
As you run these queries, think about:

  • Does the SQL feel familiar?
  • What is different from querying in SSMS?
  • What does the result tell you about the data?

docs.title: Level 1: Exploration
docs.text:
Task 1 - How many users?

SELECT COUNT(*)
FROM `bigquery-public-data.thelook_ecommerce.users`

Task 2 - How many products?

SELECT COUNT(*)
FROM `bigquery-public-data.thelook_ecommerce.products`

Task 3 - First 20 products

SELECT *
FROM `bigquery-public-data.thelook_ecommerce.products`
LIMIT 20

Task 4 - Order statuses

SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS total
FROM `bigquery-public-data.thelook_ecommerce.orders`
GROUP BY status
ORDER BY total DESC

Task 5 - Users from Germany

SELECT *
FROM `bigquery-public-data.thelook_ecommerce.users`
WHERE country = 'Germany'

docs.title: Level 2: Filtering and sorting
docs.text:
Task 6 - Jeans sorted by price

SELECT *
FROM `bigquery-public-data.thelook_ecommerce.products`
WHERE category = 'Jeans'
ORDER BY retail_price DESC

Task 7 - Returned orders

SELECT *
FROM `bigquery-public-data.thelook_ecommerce.orders`
WHERE status = 'Returned'

Task 8 - 10 most expensive products

SELECT *
FROM `bigquery-public-data.thelook_ecommerce.products`
ORDER BY retail_price DESC
LIMIT 10

Task 9 - Female users who joined after 2020

SELECT *
FROM `bigquery-public-data.thelook_ecommerce.users`
WHERE gender = 'F'
  AND created_at > '2020-12-31'

Task 10 - Order items with sale price > 100

SELECT *
FROM `bigquery-public-data.thelook_ecommerce.order_items`
WHERE sale_price > 100

docs.title: Level 3: Aggregations
docs.text:
Task 11 - Orders per user, top 20

SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count
FROM `bigquery-public-data.thelook_ecommerce.orders`
GROUP BY user_id
ORDER BY order_count DESC
LIMIT 20

Task 12 - Total revenue by product category

SELECT product_category, ROUND(SUM(sale_price), 2) AS total_revenue
FROM `bigquery-public-data.thelook_ecommerce.order_items`
GROUP BY product_category
ORDER BY total_revenue DESC

Task 13 - Average sale price per order status

SELECT status, ROUND(AVG(sale_price), 2) AS avg_sale_price
FROM `bigquery-public-data.thelook_ecommerce.order_items`
GROUP BY status
ORDER BY avg_sale_price DESC

Task 14 - Country with most users

SELECT country, COUNT(*) AS user_count
FROM `bigquery-public-data.thelook_ecommerce.users`
GROUP BY country
ORDER BY user_count DESC
LIMIT 1

Task 15 - Brands with more than 10 products

SELECT brand, COUNT(*) AS num_products
FROM `bigquery-public-data.thelook_ecommerce.products`
GROUP BY brand
HAVING COUNT(*) > 10
ORDER BY num_products DESC

docs.title: Level 4: Joins
docs.text:
Task 16 - Orders with customer name

SELECT
  o.order_id,
  u.first_name,
  u.last_name,
  o.status,
  o.created_at
FROM `bigquery-public-data.thelook_ecommerce.orders` o
JOIN `bigquery-public-data.thelook_ecommerce.users` u
  ON o.user_id = u.id
LIMIT 20

Task 17 - Order items with product name and category

SELECT
  oi.order_id,
  p.name,
  p.category,
  oi.sale_price
FROM `bigquery-public-data.thelook_ecommerce.order_items` oi
JOIN `bigquery-public-data.thelook_ecommerce.products` p
  ON oi.product_id = p.id
LIMIT 20

Task 18 - Users who have never placed an order

SELECT
  u.id,
  u.first_name,
  u.last_name
FROM `bigquery-public-data.thelook_ecommerce.users` u
LEFT JOIN `bigquery-public-data.thelook_ecommerce.orders` o
  ON u.id = o.user_id
WHERE o.order_id IS NULL

Task 19 - Top 10 customers by total spent

SELECT
  u.first_name,
  u.last_name,
  ROUND(SUM(oi.sale_price), 2) AS total_spent
FROM `bigquery-public-data.thelook_ecommerce.order_items` oi
JOIN `bigquery-public-data.thelook_ecommerce.users` u
  ON oi.user_id = u.id
GROUP BY u.id, u.first_name, u.last_name
ORDER BY total_spent DESC
LIMIT 10

Task 20 - Orders with customer name, product name, sale price

SELECT
  o.order_id,
  u.first_name,
  u.last_name,
  p.name AS product,
  p.category,
  oi.sale_price
FROM `bigquery-public-data.thelook_ecommerce.orders` o
JOIN `bigquery-public-data.thelook_ecommerce.users` u
  ON o.user_id = u.id
JOIN `bigquery-public-data.thelook_ecommerce.order_items` oi
  ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
JOIN `bigquery-public-data.thelook_ecommerce.products` p
  ON oi.product_id = p.id
LIMIT 20

docs.title: Level 5: Stretch
docs.text:
Task 21 - Most popular product category per country

Uses a CTE and RANK() window function to find the top category per country.

WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT
    u.country,
    p.category,
    COUNT(*) AS items_sold,
    RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY u.country ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC) AS rnk
  FROM `bigquery-public-data.thelook_ecommerce.order_items` oi
  JOIN `bigquery-public-data.thelook_ecommerce.users` u ON oi.user_id = u.id
  JOIN `bigquery-public-data.thelook_ecommerce.products` p ON oi.product_id = p.id
  GROUP BY u.country, p.category
)
SELECT country, category, items_sold
FROM ranked
WHERE rnk = 1
ORDER BY country

Task 22 - Percentage of orders returned

COUNTIF is a BigQuery-specific function.

SELECT
  ROUND(100.0 * COUNTIF(status = 'Returned') / COUNT(*), 2) AS pct_returned
FROM `bigquery-public-data.thelook_ecommerce.orders`

Task 23 - Month-by-month revenue trend

SELECT
  FORMAT_TIMESTAMP('%Y-%m', created_at) AS month,
  ROUND(SUM(sale_price), 2) AS revenue
FROM `bigquery-public-data.thelook_ecommerce.order_items`
GROUP BY month
ORDER BY month

Task 24 - Distribution centre with most products

SELECT
  dc.name,
  COUNT(*) AS num_items
FROM `bigquery-public-data.thelook_ecommerce.inventory_items` ii
JOIN `bigquery-public-data.thelook_ecommerce.distribution_centers` dc
  ON ii.product_distribution_center_id = dc.id
GROUP BY dc.name
ORDER BY num_items DESC

Task 25 - Create a view of completed orders

The view is created in the course project, not in bigquery-public-data. The thelook dataset must exist in ingwane-da4m3 first (create it in the console, location: US).

CREATE VIEW `ingwane-da4m3.thelook.completed_orders` AS
SELECT
  o.order_id,
  u.first_name,
  u.last_name,
  p.name AS product,
  p.category,
  oi.sale_price,
  o.created_at
FROM `bigquery-public-data.thelook_ecommerce.orders` o
JOIN `bigquery-public-data.thelook_ecommerce.users` u ON o.user_id = u.id
JOIN `bigquery-public-data.thelook_ecommerce.order_items` oi ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
JOIN `bigquery-public-data.thelook_ecommerce.products` p ON oi.product_id = p.id
WHERE o.status = 'Complete'

docs.title: Beyond the Relational Database
docs.text:
A data analyst doesn't always get to choose where the data lives - you need to recognise different types of database and know what each one is good for.

In pairs, investigate the two tools below and be ready to explain them to the room.

Pair 1: SQL Server + Cloud SQL ~ relational

Pair 2: MongoDB + Firestore ~ NoSQL / document

Pair 3: BigQuery + Snowflake ~ cloud data warehouse

Pair 4: Google Cloud Storage + Amazon S3 ~ object storage

Pair 5: Bigtable + Cassandra ~ distributed / wide-column

docs.title: Report Back
docs.text:
For your two tools, prepare a short explanation covering:

  • What type of database or storage is it?
  • What kind of data does it store best?
  • When would a data analyst need to work with this type of store?

docs.title: Framing - Yesterday Local, Today Cloud
docs.text:
Frame it as a continuation, not a new course.

Start with:

"Yesterday we worked with SQL in a local database environment. Today we are going to move that thinking beyond the local machine. The important point is not that you become experts in any particular cloud platform. The point is that SQL, tables, relationships and analysis do not disappear when the data lives somewhere else."

Then pause and ask:

"When the database is no longer local, what do you think changes?"

Let them answer. Capture just a few. Then say:

"Most of the things that change are around the database - access, location, permissions, scale, sharing. The SQL thinking itself stays surprisingly familiar."

docs.title: The opening idea
docs.text:
You want them to feel:

"I am not starting again."

Show this comparison:

Yesterday Today SQL in SSMS SQL in cloud platforms Local database Data hosted elsewhere Query results in a grid Query results in a grid or report Tables, rows, columns Tables, rows, columns SELECT, WHERE, JOIN, GROUP BY SELECT, WHERE, JOIN, GROUP BY

Then land on:

"The platform changes. The SQL thinking travels with you."

docs.title: Opening question
docs.text:
Use this one:

"Which parts of yesterday's SQL do you think will still matter today?"

This gets them to name the transfer:

  • Tables
  • Columns
  • Data types
  • Filters
  • Joins
  • Aggregations
  • Checking results
  • Asking good questions

Then say:

"Exactly. Those are the things we are carrying with us today."

docs.title: Day purpose
docs.text:
Put this on the slide:

Today's question: Where can SQL take us when the data is not just sitting on our own machine?

By the end of today, you should be able to recognise familiar database and SQL ideas across different cloud-style environments.

docs.title: What not to say
docs.text:
Avoid opening with:

"Today we are doing Google Cloud."

That sounds like a platform course. Better:

"Today we are taking SQL beyond the local machine. Google BigQuery will be our first example."

docs.title: ERD Revision: Table Design Scenarios
docs.text: Pick one scenario below and design an ERD for it: identify the entities, their attributes, primary keys, foreign keys, and the relationships (with cardinality) between them.

docs.title: Group A: Library Management System
docs.text: We need a database to manage our library's books, members, copies, and loans. Each book has an ISBN, title, author, genre, and publication year. For each member we assign a membership number, and we need to store their name, address, and contact number. Each copy represents a physical instance of a book, with a unique barcode, the book it represents, condition status, and shelf location. Finally, loans all have unique IDs, recording which member borrowed which copy, along with the loan date and due date.

docs.title: Group B: Restaurant Reservation System
docs.text: We need a database to handle our restaurant's menu items, customers, tables, and reservations. Each menu item has a unique code, name, category, price, and description of ingredients. For each customer we create a customer ID, and we need to store their name, phone number, and email address. Each table in the restaurant has a table number, seating capacity, location in the restaurant, and status. Finally, reservations all have unique IDs, specifying which customer has booked which table, along with the date, time, and party size.

docs.title: Group C: Vehicle Hire System
docs.text: We need a database to manage our hire vehicles, clients, bookings, and rental agreements. Each vehicle has a registration number, make, model, vehicle type, and daily hire rate. For each client we assign a client number, and we need to store their name, driving licence number, and contact details. Each booking represents a potential hire with a booking reference, the client making the booking, requested dates, and pickup location. Finally, rental agreements all have unique IDs, linking a confirmed booking to a specific vehicle, with actual pickup date and expected return date.

docs.title: Group D: Conference Management System
docs.text: We need a database to organise our conferences, delegates, sessions, and registrations. Each conference has a unique code, title, organising body, duration in days, and theme description. For each delegate we allocate a delegate number, and we need to store their name, organisation, and email address. Each session is a presentation within a specific conference, with a session ID, scheduled date/time, the conference it belongs to, and the venue room. Finally, registrations all have unique IDs, recording which delegate is attending which session.

docs.title: ERD Revision: Approach
docs.text:
A quick recap of the process before you start on your scenario.

  1. Identify the entities. Read the scenario and pick out the nouns that need their own table (e.g. Book, Member).
  2. Identify the attributes. For each entity, list the pieces of data it needs to store.
  3. Identify the primary key. Pick (or add) the attribute that uniquely identifies each row.
  4. Identify the relationships. Work out how entities connect, and the cardinality of each (one-to-many, many-to-many, etc.).
  5. Add the foreign keys. For a one-to-many relationship, the FK goes on the "many" side. For a many-to-many relationship, add a junction table.

Work through your scenario in this order - don't jump straight to drawing boxes and lines.

docs.title: MongoDB Labs ~ NoSQL Fundamentals
docs.text:
Runs on Firestore with MongoDB compatibility - a native Google Cloud database (Firestore, Enterprise edition) that accepts MongoDB's own query language. No Docker, no local server - mongosh on the VM connects over the network to a database sitting in your GCP project, the same way you connected to BigQuery.

Trainer: confirm before delivery

This GCP feature only went GA August 2025, so it hasn't been run in this course before. Before the day, check: Firestore Enterprise edition is enabled/billable in the training GCP project, mongosh installs cleanly on the VM image, and decide whether each learner gets their own database or a shared database with one collection per learner (e.g. customers_<name>).

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
• Login to your Virtual Machine
  • Open Terminal / PowerShell
  • Check whether mongosh is already installed: mongosh --version
    • If not, install it (e.g. winget install MongoDB.Shell --source winget on Windows, or download from mongodb.com/try/download/shell)
    • The --source winget flag avoids a certificate error some lab VMs hit when winget also tries the msstore source
    • After installing, close the terminal window and open a new one before running mongosh --version again - an already-open shell doesn't pick up the PATH update, and will report mongosh as not recognized

docs.title: Instructor Led Demo
docs.text:
Create the database (Google Cloud Console or Cloud Shell)

# Create a Firestore Enterprise database with MongoDB compatibility enabled
gcloud firestore databases create \
  --database=shop \
  --edition=enterprise \
  --location=YOUR-REGION \
  --enable-mongodb-compatible-data-access

# Create a database user (prints the generated password - save it, it can't be retrieved again)
gcloud firestore user-creds create trainer --database=shop

One-off setup

This only needs doing once (by the trainer, in the shared training project) - not per learner, unless you decide each learner should have their own database.

Get the connection string

In the Cloud Console: Firestore > Databases > shop > Connect, choose mongosh, and copy the generated command. It will look like:

mongosh 'mongodb://USERNAME:PASSWORD@CONNECTION_STRING:443/shop?loadBalanced=true&authMechanism=SCRAM-SHA-256&tls=true&retryWrites=false'

Run that in the terminal to connect. Keep the single quotes around the whole string.

You should see the MongoDB shell prompt: > (or shop>)

Insert First Document

Note

No use shop step needed here - the connection string already connects you straight into the shop database that was created via gcloud.

// Insert a customer document
db.customers.insertOne({
  name: "Sarah Johnson",
  email: "sarah@example.com",
  age: 32,
  city: "London"
})

// See what we created
db.customers.find()

Note

We didn't create a table structure first - just inserted data!

docs.title: Hands-On Practice ~ Learners
docs.text:
Task 1: Insert Different Customer Structures

Insert these three customers:

// Customer 1: Basic info
db.customers.insertOne({
  name: "James Smith",
  email: "james@example.com",
  age: 28
})

// Customer 2: Has additional phone and country fields
db.customers.insertOne({
  name: "Priya Patel",
  email: "priya@example.com",
  age: 35,
  phone: "020-1234-5678",
  country: "UK"
})

// Customer 3: Completely different structure - business customer
db.customers.insertOne({
  companyName: "Tech Solutions Ltd",
  contactPerson: "Michael Chen",
  email: "michael@techsolutions.com",
  employees: 50,
  accountType: "business"
})

Note

See how each customer has different fields - this is the power of flexible schema!

Task 2: View All Customers

// Get all customers
db.customers.find()

// Make it prettier (easier to read)
db.customers.find().pretty()

Task 3: Explore What You Created

// See all databases
show dbs

// See collections in current database
show collections

// Count how many customers you have
db.customers.countDocuments({})

// Rough count without scanning everything (for big collections)
db.customers.estimatedDocumentCount()

docs.title: Discussion
docs.text:
Questions to explore:

  • What happens if you try to query for a field that doesn't exist in some documents?
  • How is this different from SQL tables where every row must have the same columns?
  • When might flexible schema be useful?

docs.title: Instructor Led Demo
docs.text:
Finding Documents with Filters

// Find all customers
db.customers.find()

// Find customers in London
db.customers.find({ "city": "London" })

// Find customers in country UK (field town does not exist)
db.customers.find({ "town": "London Town" })

// Find customers older than 30
db.customers.find({ "age": { $gt: 30 } })

// Find customers with age between 25 and 35
db.customers.find({ "age": { $gte: 25, $lte: 35 } })

Updating Documents

// Sarah's current details
db.customers.find({ "name": "Sarah Johnson" })

// Update Sarah's city
db.customers.updateOne(
  { "name": "Sarah Johnson" },
  { $set: { "city": "Manchester" } }
)

// Verify the update
db.customers.find({ "name": "Sarah Johnson" })

docs.title: Hands-On Practice ~ Learners
docs.text:
Task 1: Practice Finding

// Find customer by name
db.customers.findOne({ "name": "James Smith" })

// Find all customers who have a phone field
db.customers.find({ "phone": { $exists: true } })

// Find business customers (accountType is "business")
db.customers.find({ "accountType": "business" })

Task 2: Update Customer Information

// Add a phone number to James Smith
db.customers.updateOne(
  { "name": "James Smith" },
  { $set: { "phone": "020-9876-5432" } }
)

// Add a new field "memberSince" to Priya
db.customers.updateOne(
  { name: "Priya Patel" },
  { $set: { "memberSince": "2024-01-15" } }
)

// Check your updates
db.customers.find().pretty()

Task 3: Delete Documents

// Delete Tech Solutions Ltd
db.customers.deleteOne({ "companyName": "Tech Solutions Ltd" })

// Verify deletion
db.customers.countDocuments({})

docs.title: Discussion
docs.text:
Key Observations:

  • What happened when you added a phone field to James? Did it affect other customers?
  • MongoDB let you add fields that don't exist - is this good or bad?

docs.title: Instructor Led Demo
docs.text:
The Power of Embedding

In traditional databases, you'd have a customers table and an orders table, then JOIN them.

In MongoDB, you can embed orders directly inside the customer document.

// Insert a customer with embedded orders
db.customers.insertOne({
  name: "Emma Wilson",
  email: "emma@example.com",
  city: "Birmingham",
  orders: [
    {
      orderId: "ORD001",
      date: "2024-11-01",
      items: ["Laptop", "Mouse"],
      total: 899.99
    },
    {
      orderId: "ORD002",
      date: "2024-11-10",
      items: ["Keyboard"],
      total: 79.99
    }
  ]
})

Query Embedded Data

// Find Emma and see all her orders
db.customers.find({ "name": "Emma Wilson" }).pretty()

// Find customers who have orders
db.customers.find({ "orders": { $exists: true } }).pretty()

// Find customers with orders over £500
db.customers.find({ "orders.total": { $gt: 500 } }).pretty()

docs.title: Hands-On Practice ~ Learners
docs.text:
Task 1: Create Customer with Orders

Create a new customer with their order history embedded:

db.customers.insertOne({
  name: "David Thompson",
  email: "david@example.com",
  city: "Leeds",
  memberSince: "2023-06-15",
  orders: [
    {
      orderId: "ORD003",
      date: "2024-10-15",
      items: ["Monitor", "HDMI Cable"],
      total: 249.99
    },
    {
      orderId: "ORD004",
      date: "2024-11-05",
      items: ["Webcam"],
      total: 89.99
    },
    {
      orderId: "ORD005",
      date: "2024-11-12",
      items: ["Desk Lamp", "USB Hub"],
      total: 45.50
    }
  ]
})

Task 2: Query Embedded Data

// Find David's complete record
db.customers.find({ "name": "David Thompson" }).pretty()

// Find customers with more than 2 orders
db.customers.find({ "orders.2": { $exists: true } })

// Find customers who ordered in November 2024
db.customers.find({ "orders.date": { $regex: "2024-11" } })

Task 3: Update Embedded Data

// Add a new order to Emma
db.customers.updateOne(
  { name: "Emma Wilson" },
  { 
    $push: { 
      orders: {
        orderId: "ORD006",
        date: "2024-11-14",
        items: ["Phone Case"],
        total: 15.99
      }
    }
  }
)

// Check the update
db.customers.find({ "name": "Emma Wilson" }).pretty()

docs.title: Discussion
docs.text:
When to Embed vs When to Reference?

  • Embedded orders work great here - why?
  • What if a customer had 10,000 orders? Still embed?
  • What if multiple customers could share the same order? (e.g., group orders)

Note

MongoDB gives you flexibility - choose based on your query patterns and data size.

docs.title: What We've Learned
docs.text:
1. Flexible Schema: Documents in the same collection can have different fields

  2. Easy CRUD: Insert, find, update, delete - simple operations

  3. Embedding: Store related data together without joins

  4. When to Use MongoDB:

    • Rapidly changing requirements
    • Varied data structures
    • Read-heavy workloads
    • Horizontal scaling needs

docs.title: Quick Reference Commands
docs.text:
// Database operations
use <database>              // Switch to database
show dbs                    // List databases
db.dropDatabase()           // Delete current database

// Collection operations
show collections           // List collections
db.<collection>.drop()     // Delete collection

// CRUD operations
db.<collection>.insertOne({})                // Insert one document
db.<collection>.find()                       // Find all documents
db.<collection>.find({ field: value })       // Find with filter
db.<collection>.updateOne({}, { $set: {} })  // Update document
db.<collection>.deleteOne({})                // Delete document

// Useful queries
db.<collection>.countDocuments()           // Count documents
db.<collection>.find().pretty()            // Format output nicely
db.<collection>.find().limit(5)            // Limit results
db.<collection>.find().sort({ field: 1 })  // Sort (1=asc, -1=desc)

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
mongosh not found?

Install it - see Initial Setup above.

Can't connect / authentication fails?

  • Re-copy the connection string from Firestore > Databases > shop > Connect in the console - the password isn't recoverable if lost, so a new user may be needed via gcloud firestore user-creds create.
  • Check the connection string still has loadBalanced=true&tls=true&retryWrites=false - these are required, not optional.

Want to start fresh?

# Delete all documents in the collection without deleting the database
db.customers.deleteMany({})

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: This one-day instructor-led class provides an overview of Google Cloud Platform products and services. Through a combination of presentations, demos, and hands-on labs, participants learn the value of Google Cloud Platform and how to incorporate cloud-based solutions into business strategies.

docs.title: Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
• Identify the purpose and value of Google Cloud Platform products and services
  • Interact with Google Cloud Platform services
  • Describe ways in which customers have used Google Cloud Platform
  • Choose among and use application deployment environments on Google Cloud Platform: Google App Engine, Google Container Engine, and Google Compute Engine
  • Choose among and use Google Cloud Platform storage options: Google Cloud Storage, Google Cloud SQL, Google Cloud Bigtable, and Google Cloud Datastore
  • Make basic use of BigQuery, Google’s managed data warehouse for analytics

docs.title: Introducing Google Cloud Platform
docs.text: Google Cloud Platform offers four main kinds of services: Compute, Storage, Big Data, and Machine Learning. This course focuses mostly on the first two, together with Google Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) networking. This module orients learners to the basics of Google Cloud Platform. It traces the evolution of cloud computing and explains what is unique about Google's approach to it. The module introduces the key structural concepts of regions and zones.

docs.title: Getting Started with Google Cloud Platform
docs.text: GCP customers use projects to organize the resources they use. They use Google Cloud Identity and Access Management, also called “IAM,” to control who can do what with those resources. They use any of several technologies to connect with GCP. This module covers each of these topics, and it introduces a service called Cloud Launcher that is an easy way to get started with GCP.

docs.title: Virtual Machines in the Cloud
docs.text: Compute Engine lets you run virtual machines on Google’s global infrastructure. This module covers how Compute Engine works, with a focus on Google virtual networking.

docs.title: Storage in the Cloud
docs.text: Every application needs to store data. Different applications and workloads require different storage and database solutions. This module describes and differentiates among GCP's core storage options: Cloud Storage, Cloud SQL, Cloud Spanner, Cloud Datastore, and Google Bigtable.

docs.title: Containers in the Cloud
docs.text: Containers are simple and interoperable, and they enable seamless, fine-grained scaling. Kubernetes is an orchestration layer for containers. Kubernetes Engine is Kubernetes as a service, a scalable managed offering that runs on Google’s infrastructure. You direct the creation of a cluster, and Kubernetes Engine schedules your containers into the cluster and manages them automatically, based on requirements you define. This module explains how Kubernetes Engine works and how it helps deploy applications in containers.

docs.title: Applications in the Cloud
docs.text: App Engine is a Platform-as-a-Service ('PaaS') offering. The App Engine platform manages the hardware and networking infrastructure required to run your code. App Engine provides built-in services that many web applications need. This module describes how App Engine works.

docs.title: Developing, Deploying and Monitoring in the Cloud
docs.text: Popular tools for development, deployment, and monitoring just work in GCP. Customers also have options for tools in each of these three areas that are tightly integrated with GCP. This module covers those tools.

docs.title: Big Data and Machine Learning in the Cloud
docs.text: GCP's big-data and machine learning offerings are intended to help customers get the most out of data. These tools are intended to be simple and practical to embed in your applications. This module describes the available big-data and machine learning services and explains the usefulness of each.

docs.title: Summary and Review
docs.text:
This module reviews the GCP services covered in this course and reminds learners of the differences among them. The module compares GCP compute services, GCP storage services, and important Google VPC networking capabilities.
